extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and applying Kant's criteria for aesthetic judgement, especially the distinctions and requirements for calling something 'beautiful' or 'sublime' and the conditions that make such judgements claim universal assent. Focus is on pure (a priori) aesthetic judgements about nature, feeling, and moral relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautiful — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Beautiful is what pleases in the mere judgement (and therefore not by the medium of sensation in accordance with a concept of the Understanding). It must please apart from all interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise 'mere judgement' and 'disinterested' pleasure: an object called beautiful should please without reference to desire, gratification, or a concept of purpose. Examples: beauty of nature perceived without teleological thought. Avoid grounding beauty in sensation-based gratifications or in purposes (teleological accounts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sublime is what pleases immediately through its opposition to the interest of sense. It is an object the representation of which determines the mind to think the unattainability of nature regarded as a presentation of Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity arises when the imagination is strained by ideas of absolute totality or magnitude (mathematical or dynamical), generating a 'negative' satisfaction: a feeling of deprivation or awe that nevertheless expands the mind. Examples: mountain peaks, deep chasms, the starry heaven, the ocean (when conceived merely as what strikes the eye).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of aesthetic judgement (freedom from concepts and interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pure aesthetical judgement must not be determined by sensation or by concepts (e.g., teleological considerations). It must be a formal, not teleological or merely sensual, judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging beauty or sublimity, do not introduce concepts of purpose, utility, or moral/teleological narratives about the object (e.g., do not imagine stars as suns for inhabitants). Such additions make the judgement impure. Evaluate objects 'just as we see them' to preserve purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic purposiveness (formal purposiveness of the object)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical purposiveness is the conformity to law of the Judgement in its freedom: objects may be represented as subjectively purposive for our cognitive faculties without being objectively purposeful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the object's form accommodates the faculties of imagination and understanding in free play (purposiveness without a concept). This is the basis for calling something aesthetically fitting even though no determinate concept of purpose is involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim to universal assent (a priori universality of taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste determines its object in respect of satisfaction with an accompanying claim for the assent of every one, just as if it were objective; it presumes a priori universal validity even though it is not cognitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making or evaluating an aesthetic claim, be aware that taste purports to be universally valid (not merely subjective). This is why Kant seeks a Deduction: the critic should test whether the judgement can legitimately demand universal agreement despite not being conceptual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of taste (a priori individual judgement)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is required that the subject shall judge by himself, without needing to grope about empirically among the judgements of others; his judgement should be pronounced a priori and not be mere imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a judgement arises from the subject's independent taste (autonomy) rather than conformity to public opinion or imitation. 'Following' exemplary works is acceptable as guidance, but imitation or heteronomy undermines pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indeterminability by grounds of proof (subjectivity without proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is not determinable by grounds of proof, just as if it were merely subjective; a hundred voices praising will not compel inner agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that aesthetic judgements cannot be validated by logical proofs or empirical confirmation alone. Critiques should therefore focus on the subject's experience of free play and communicability rather than adducing objective proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative vs positive satisfaction (Sublime vs Beautiful)
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the Sublime of nature is negative (the Imagination feels deprived even while enlarged), whilst that in the Beautiful is positive (a direct pleasantness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish feelings: beautiful objects give immediate positive pleasure; sublime objects provoke a pleasurable sense of limitation or struggle in the imagination (awe, astonishment bordering on terror, but not actual fear). Use this as a diagnostic when classifying experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral connection of the Sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: A feeling for the Sublime in nature cannot well be thought without combining therewith a mental disposition which is akin to the Moral; the Sublime prepares us to esteem something highly even in opposition to sensible interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess sublimity partly via its relation to moral ideas: experiences that awaken the mind's sense of supersensible ends, respect for moral law, or capacity to overcome sensibility are more properly sublime. Intellectual, moral greatness (e.g., self-command, noble apathy) is aesthetically sublime rather than beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teleological or purposive concepts when judging nature's beauty/sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of nature called sublime must be judged 'just as we see it' and not by supplying teleological concepts (e.g., regarding stars as suns for inhabitants) since that would make the judgement teleological, not purely aesthetical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating natural objects, strip away background knowledge of functions or purposes. Judge the visual/formal presentation alone to preserve the purity of the aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional quality criteria: strenuous vs languid affections
rubrics_metrics.description: Affections of the strenuous kind (exciting consciousness of our power to overcome obstacles) are aesthetically sublime (e.g., wrath, indignation); affections of the languid kind (making resistance an object of pain) belong to the sensuously beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify emotional states elicited by works or experiences: strong, overcoming emotions can ground sublime responses; weak, languid sentimental emotions indicate sensuous beauty or sentimentality rather than sublime nobility. Be wary of sentimentalism that produces mere languor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as style for the Sublime and moral presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity (purposiveness without art) is the style of Nature in the sublime, and so also of Morality which is a second (supersensible) nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value unadorned, artless representations where purposiveness appears without contrivance when aiming for sublimity or moral grandeur. Excessive ornamentation may undercut the sublimity that simplicity secures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicability and social interest of the Beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in the Beautiful is distinguishable by its universal communicability and thereby acquires an interest in reference to society (in which this communication is possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether an aesthetic judgement is communicable (can be shared and discussed); beauty that fosters social communication supports the claim to universality of taste. Conversely, certain forms of solitude or self-sufficiency may be sublime rather than socially beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of empirical/physiological accounts (critique of Burke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical physiological accounts (e.g., Burke's linkage of the Sublime to fear/self-preservation and the Beautiful to bodily relaxation) are valuable as psychology but cannot ground the a priori universal validity of aesthetic judgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce aesthetic judgement to mere physiological responses when asserting universal validity; such empirical explanations explain how we judge but not how we ought to judge. Use empirical observations as material, not as justificatory foundations for claims of necessary validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction requirement for judgements of Taste (Beautiful in nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim of an aesthetical judgement to universal validity for every subject requires, as a judgement resting on some a priori principle, a Deduction (legitimating its pretensions) in addition to its Exposition; this is required particularly for judgements about the Beautiful in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a critic or theorist asserts necessary or universal validity for aesthetic judgements (especially about natural beauty), they should offer a 'Deduction'—an account showing how the judgement rests on a priori grounds (i.e., how subjective purposiveness can claim universality). For the Sublime, Kant considers the exposition already serves as its deduction.
